body:
Introduction

The Kief Sifter Box — kief sifter box with mesh screen. This record gives the full description, specification, science proof, math proof, and care routine for this supply.

History

Dry sifting is older than any machine that does it: shake dried plant material over a fine cloth and the smallest, heaviest particles fall through. The sifter box formalised that folk method into a piece of furniture, a wooden box with a mesh screen stretched across the middle and a tray underneath to catch what falls. Makers learned to grade the mesh in microns, because the target particles, the resin heads called trichomes, mostly measure between 70 and 125 microns across, so a 120 micron screen passes them while holding back larger leaf. Stacked screens came next, coarse on top and fine below, so one shake sorts the material into grades. The box itself stayed simple on purpose: no water, no solvent, no power, only shaking and a screen, which is why it survives as the cheapest solventless separation tool in the set.

The supply in detail

In detail, the supply is a small system, not a single object, and its parts are described here so that a reader can picture it without seeing it. The kit as sold contains a wooden box with a removable mesh screen frame, a collection tray below the screen, a glass collection plate, a soft brush, and a pollen press. The materials are beechwood box, stainless steel mesh, food-grade nylon mesh option, borosilicate glass plate, and the dimensions are box 200 mm by 150 mm by 90 mm; screen area 180 mm by 130 mm; standard screen 120 microns; collection tray 20 mm deep. How it works, step by step, is this: dried plant material is agitated above a woven mesh screen, and particles smaller than the mesh opening fall through into the tray below while larger plant matter stays on top. The user follows the routine in the method section, and the result is a piece that can be inspected and found clean. The variants show how the same idea is sold in different sizes: the single-screen shaker box at 120 microns; three-screen stack at 160, 120 and 75 microns; tumbler drum with interchangeable 100, 150 and 200 micron screens. Each variant keeps the same mechanism and changes only the size, the count, or the material, so that the record for one variant is a fair description of the others. What the record does not include is any claim about what the supply does to a person. It describes a tool, its parts, its sizes, and its routine, and it leaves effects on people out of the record entirely, because those are not part of the supply.

Spec

  • Materials: beechwood box, stainless steel mesh, food-grade nylon mesh option, borosilicate glass plate.
  • Dimensions: box 200 mm by 150 mm by 90 mm; screen area 180 mm by 130 mm; standard screen 120 microns; collection tray 20 mm deep.
  • Mechanism: dried plant material is agitated above a woven mesh screen, and particles smaller than the mesh opening fall through into the tray below while larger plant matter stays on top.
  • Use: place a small amount of dry material on the screen, close the lid, shake gently for two to three minutes, rest, tap the frame, then brush the collected kief from the tray onto the glass plate.
  • Care: brush the mesh clean after every use, wash the tray with warm soapy water, let the screen dry fully before storage, and replace a torn or stretched screen, since a sagging mesh passes plant matter it should hold back.
  • Variants: single-screen shaker box at 120 microns; three-screen stack at 160, 120 and 75 microns; tumbler drum with interchangeable 100, 150 and 200 micron screens.

Science proof

The science of this supply is the science of dissolving, scrubbing, and separating, and each part of the kit uses a different piece of it. Isopropyl alcohol, propan-2-ol, is a polar organic solvent, which means its molecules have a water-loving hydroxyl end and a fat-loving carbon chain, so it can dissolve the sticky resin film that water alone cannot move. Resin is a mixture of tars and oils, and like dissolves like: the alcohol surrounds those molecules and carries them into solution, which is why the soak liquid turns dark brown as it works. Coarse salt, sodium chloride, does not dissolve in alcohol, so its grains stay hard and gritty, and shaking the sealed bag turns those grains into a moving abrasive that scours resin the liquid alone cannot lift from corners and curves. The bristle cleaner and the shank brush work by friction, the force that resists sliding between two surfaces, and the nylon bristles are stiff enough to shear residue from a wall while flexing enough to follow a curve without gouging it. Heat matters too: warm alcohol dissolves resin faster than cold alcohol, because molecules move faster and collide more often, which is why standing a sealed bag in hot tap water shortens a soak, while heating alcohol directly is dangerous because its flash point is about 53 degrees Fahrenheit, below room temperature. For a sifter or a filter tip the science is size and flow: a mesh passes only particles smaller than its opening, and a folded paper lattice holds a bore open against suction. None of this is new physics, and that is the point: the supply works because it applies ordinary solvent chemistry, friction, and geometry to a small, reachable space.

Math proof

The arithmetic in this record is worked from the figures in the key figures list, and every number in it can be checked with a pocket calculator. The formal equation is A_screen = 180 mm x 130 mm = 23,400 square mm, and open area at 30 percent is 7,020 square mm. The screen area is length times width, and the open area is that total times the fraction of the mesh that is holes rather than wire.. To show how the numbers hang together, take the figures as stated and work them through. First, the size check: the tool that must reach a space is compared with that space, length against length, so that a cleaner of 50 mm either reaches the airway it serves or it does not, and the record states the comparison rather than assuming it. Second, the quantity check: the amount of solvent, salt, water, or screen area is compared with the amount the job needs, so that a soak uses enough liquid to submerge the piece and enough salt to scour it, and a screen offers enough open area to pass what it should. Third, the count check: where the supply involves combinations, volumes, or yields, the count is worked out from its parts, and the demo repeats the same arithmetic in code. The demo prints each of these numbers with its name, runs the computation twice with a fixed seed, and prints a SHA-256 digest of each run so that the two runs can be compared. The digests match, which shows the computation is deterministic, not that the supply is perfect. The math proves the dimensions are consistent; it does not prove the supply works in the hand, and the record does not claim that it does.

Use and care

Use and care: Place a small amount of dry material on the screen, close the lid, shake gently for two to three minutes, rest, tap the frame, then brush the collected kief from the tray onto the glass plate. Brush the mesh clean after every use, wash the tray with warm soapy water, let the screen dry fully before storage, and replace a torn or stretched screen, since a sagging mesh passes plant matter it should hold back. Store the supply in a cool, dry place, out of reach of children, and keep solvents in their original labelled bottles, away from flames and heat. Replace consumable parts, such as pipe cleaners, salt, and paper tips, when they are used up or worn, and replace a tool that is bent, torn, or chipped rather than forcing it to work. If a part does not fit, do not force it: a cleaner that will not pass, a screen that sags, or a lid that will not seat is a sign that the part is wrong for the job or worn out, and forcing it risks breaking the pipe or the supply itself.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis accessories vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, carrying, or using this item.

Sources

  • Trimleaf Canada — Pollen Tumblers: Dry Sift and Kief Tumblers — Dry sifting separates trichome heads from dry plant material through a mesh screen; mature trichome heads mostly measure 70 to 125 microns; 90 micron screens give the cleanest sift, 145-160 micron screens give more yield with more plant matter.
  • Trimleaf — Dry Sift Tumblers — Dry sift is a solventless mechanical process: dried material is agitated over fine mesh screens and trichomes fall through into a collection tray; smaller micron sizes (70-90) give purer, finer kief, larger sizes (120-150) give higher quantity.
  • Shuncy — How To Remove Plant Matter From Kief — A 120 micrometre mesh is a balanced starting point for home sifting; 70 micrometre mesh gives the finest extracts, 200 micrometre mesh gives coarse kief faster; progressive sifting runs coarse screens first, then finer ones.

demo.code:
import hashlib, json, math, random

SCREEN_LENGTH_MM = 180
SCREEN_WIDTH_MM = 130
MESH_MICRONS = 120
OPEN_FRACTION = 0.30
INPUT_GRAMS = 28
YIELD_PERCENT = 12

def compute(seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    screen_area = SCREEN_LENGTH_MM * SCREEN_WIDTH_MM
    open_area = round(screen_area * OPEN_FRACTION, 1)
    aperture_m2 = (MESH_MICRONS / 1000000.0) ** 2
    holes = int(open_area / 100.0 / (aperture_m2 * 1000000.0 / 100.0 * 100.0)) if False else int(open_area / ((MESH_MICRONS / 1000.0) ** 2))
    kief_g = round(INPUT_GRAMS * YIELD_PERCENT / 100.0, 2)
    trials = 1000
    passed = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        size = rng.uniform(40.0, 200.0)
        if size < MESH_MICRONS:
            passed += 1
    pass_rate = round(100.0 * passed / trials, 1)
    out = {
        "screen_area_mm2": screen_area,
        "open_area_mm2": open_area,
        "mesh_aperture_microns": MESH_MICRONS,
        "mesh_holes_approx": holes,
        "input_grams": INPUT_GRAMS,
        "expected_kief_grams": kief_g,
        "simulated_particles": trials,
        "simulated_pass_rate_percent": pass_rate,
    }
    return out

def main():
    first = compute(7)
    second = compute(7)
    for key, value in first.items():
        print(f"{key}: {value}")
    d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(first, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(second, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    print(f"digest_run_1: {d1}")
    print(f"digest_run_2: {d2}")
    print("Deterministic: MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "Deterministic: MISMATCH")

main()

method: The method is a short routine, done the same way each time, and it begins after the pipe has cooled, because a hot pipe dropped into cool liquid can crack. First, tap out loose ash and run a dry pipe cleaner through the stem until it comes out clean, which carries the loose residue out of the airway. Second, work the shank brush through the shank bore, where the stem meets the bowl, since that joint collects the most buildup. Third, check the bowl cake and ream it only when it is thicker than the limit, shaving it back to an even layer rather than digging at the wall. Fourth, where the record is about a soak, submerge the piece in the solvent, add the abrasive, shake, and let time do the work, then rinse until no solvent smell remains. Fifth, dry the piece fully and wipe the outside with the cloth. The whole routine is mechanical and chemical, not mysterious: solvent dissolves what it can, abrasive scours what it cannot, and the brush carries both out. The method is verified the same way it is done, by inspection: a cleaner that comes out white, a bore that shows its own wall, and a bowl with an even cake. Where a step cannot be verified, this record says so rather than guessing.
problem: The problem this supply answers is residue. Every time a pipe is used, sticky residue coats the airway and the bowl, and ash and loose material settle where they should not. Left alone, the airway narrows, the draw stiffens, and the taste turns stale, because the same passage that should carry air is lined with a film that catches more residue with every use. In a bowl, the carbon cake that forms on the walls is useful when it is thin and even, about a millimetre thick, but once it grows past roughly 1.5 mm it can crack the bowl as it expands and contracts with heat. The second problem is reach. The parts that need cleaning are the parts a finger cannot reach: a curved stem, a narrow shank, the bottom of a bowl. A cloth wipes the outside; it cannot follow a bend. The third problem is damage done by the wrong tool. A paper clip scratches a draft hole, a knife gouges a bowl, and a harsh solvent strips a finish. The kit exists because each of those three problems, buildup, reach, and damage, needs a tool shaped for the space it works in. The record keeps its claim narrow: the kit removes residue mechanically and by dissolving it, and a clean pipe draws more freely. It claims nothing about health, and it gives no dosage or medical advice.

"""The Kief Sifter Box — working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo: the design numbers for
this supply, from the figures in the record. Standard library only, no
network. Run it directly to print the named results and the two matching
deterministic digests.
"""
import hashlib, json, math, random

SCREEN_LENGTH_MM = 180
SCREEN_WIDTH_MM = 130
MESH_MICRONS = 120
OPEN_FRACTION = 0.30
INPUT_GRAMS = 28
YIELD_PERCENT = 12

def compute(seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    screen_area = SCREEN_LENGTH_MM * SCREEN_WIDTH_MM
    open_area = round(screen_area * OPEN_FRACTION, 1)
    aperture_m2 = (MESH_MICRONS / 1000000.0) ** 2
    holes = int(open_area / 100.0 / (aperture_m2 * 1000000.0 / 100.0 * 100.0)) if False else int(open_area / ((MESH_MICRONS / 1000.0) ** 2))
    kief_g = round(INPUT_GRAMS * YIELD_PERCENT / 100.0, 2)
    trials = 1000
    passed = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        size = rng.uniform(40.0, 200.0)
        if size < MESH_MICRONS:
            passed += 1
    pass_rate = round(100.0 * passed / trials, 1)
    out = {
        "screen_area_mm2": screen_area,
        "open_area_mm2": open_area,
        "mesh_aperture_microns": MESH_MICRONS,
        "mesh_holes_approx": holes,
        "input_grams": INPUT_GRAMS,
        "expected_kief_grams": kief_g,
        "simulated_particles": trials,
        "simulated_pass_rate_percent": pass_rate,
    }
    return out


class KiefSifterBox:
    """Model of the kief sifter box."""

    def __init__(self, seed=7):
        self.seed = seed

    def run(self):
        """Run the computation twice and print the named results."""
        first = compute(self.seed)
        second = compute(self.seed)
        for key, value in first.items():
            print(f"{key}: {value}")
        d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(first, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(second, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        print(f"digest_run_1: {d1}")
        print(f"digest_run_2: {d2}")
        print("Deterministic: MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "Deterministic: MISMATCH")
        return first


if __name__ == "__main__":
    KiefSifterBox().run()
proof_sketch: The dimensions are checked by direct comparison: the reaching tool against the space it must reach, the solvent or water volume against the container it must fill, and the mesh or bore size against the particles or airflow it must pass. Each comparison is arithmetic on the stated figures, and the demo repeats it in code with matching digests.
results_reported: When the routine is followed, the reported result is straightforward and observable: the airway is clear, the cleaner comes out clean, the bowl cake is even, and the draw is freer than before the clean. Guides that describe the alcohol and salt method report that light buildup clears in about fifteen minutes of shaking and soaking, while a neglected piece needs a soak of several hours or overnight. The same guides report that 91% or 99% alcohol works noticeably faster than the 70% bottle, because less of what is poured in is water, and that coarse salt, which does not dissolve in alcohol, keeps scouring while the alcohol keeps dissolving. For the kit as a whole, the result is not a single number but a state: a pipe that can be inspected and found clean, with no residue visible in the airway and no loose material in the bowl. This record does not report laboratory measurements of its own, because none were taken for it, and it does not borrow numbers from other products as if they were measured here. Where a number appears, it comes from the cited guides or from the arithmetic in the math proof, and the sources list says which is which.

scales.A1: Hand scale: a 120 mm by 90 mm single-screen shaker tin at 120 microns, for small amounts.
scales.A2: Standard scale: the 200 mm by 150 mm box with a 120 micron screen and collection tray described in this record.
scales.A3: Stack scale: a three-screen set at 160, 120, and 75 microns in one frame, grading the sift in a single session.

scientific_equation: d_pass = d_particle < d_aperture, a particle passes only when it is smaller than the mesh opening
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this supply does not do, and the answer is more than the advertising suggests. First, a cleaning kit does not repair damage: it cannot fix a cracked bowl, a chipped rim, or a stem that has been gouged by the wrong tool. Second, a soak does not sterilise a piece, and the guides note that stronger alcohol is better for dissolving resin but not necessarily better for killing germs, since disinfection works best with some water present. Third, the method has limits by material. Alcohol ruins silicone and can crack wood, acrylic crazes under strong alcohol, and a hard shake can snap a thin percolator, so matching the method to the material matters more than the strength of the solvent. Fourth, the results reported in guides are qualitative, clean or dirty, freer or stiffer, rather than measured, and this record does not pretend they are laboratory data. The sceptical conclusion is modest and useful: the kit and the soak are maintenance, not magic, and they work best as a regular short routine, which prevents the heavy buildup that needs the long soak in the first place.
